Planning the second season at the orchard

Now that winter has settled in and the trees are dormant, our steering group has been meeting every other week to plan the second season. This post is a summary of where those conversations have landed, so that everyone in the neighborhood group can see what we are thinking and weigh in before we commit to anything. Nothing here is final. If you disagree with any of it, please come to the next meeting or send me a message.

The biggest decision ahead of us is the fence. Last year we put up a temporary mesh fence after the deer damage in August, and it has held up better than we expected. But it sags in several places, the posts are already leaning, and it will not survive another full year of weather. We have two quotes for a permanent fence. The cheaper one uses wooden posts and welded wire, and the more expensive one uses steel posts and a taller mesh. After a long discussion, the group is leaning toward the steel option. It costs more up front, but it should last much longer, and the extra height matters because the deer here are not shy about jumping.

To pay for it, we are planning two fundraising events. The first is a spring plant sale, where volunteers will grow seedlings at home over the winter and sell them at the library on a Saturday in April. Several people have already started trays of tomatoes, peppers, and herbs on their windowsills. The second is a fall harvest party, which we hope will be a little bigger than last year's cider evening. We will not have much fruit of our own yet, but a local farm has offered to donate apples again, and a neighbor who runs a food truck has offered to cook.

The second big decision is about the wet corner. We lost four trees there last year, and we have since dug a drainage channel. Over the winter, I have been reading about trees that handle heavy, damp soil, and the group has talked with the extension office about what might work. The current plan is to plant two quince trees and a pair of pears grafted onto rootstock that tolerates wet conditions. We will also add a raised berm along the low edge, to keep standing water away from the trunks. This is an experiment, and we will analyze how those trees do over the summer before deciding whether to use the same approach anywhere else.

The third decision is about tools and storage. Right now, volunteers carry tools to and from the orchard every work day, which is tiring and means we often arrive without something we need. We want to build a small shed near the gate. One of our members is a carpenter, and he has drawn up a simple design that we could build ourselves over two or three weekends. The library has agreed in principle to let us put it on their side of the lot line, which solves a zoning question that had worried us. We still need to buy the materials, and we are hoping a local lumber yard will donate some of them.

Beyond those three decisions, we have been talking a lot about how to keep volunteers involved. Last year we learned that a small, steady crew does most of the work, and that giving each person a specific tree or task keeps them coming back. This year we want to build on that. We are going to set up a simple sign-up sheet, posted online and at the gate, where people can claim a tree for the season. Each tree adopter will be asked to check on their tree at least twice a month, water it during dry spells, and report anything unusual in the logbook.

We also want to make the work days more welcoming for newcomers. Several people told us they felt a little lost the first time they came, while everyone else seemed to know what to do. So this year, each work day will start with a ten-minute introduction for anyone new, covering where things are, what we are working on, and who to ask for help. We will also pair new volunteers with someone experienced for their first few sessions.

The pruning workshops are confirmed. Our neighbor, the retired arborist, will lead three sessions over the late winter and early spring, while the trees are still dormant. The first will cover the basics of why and when to prune, the second will be hands-on work on our own trees, and the third will look at how to train young trees into a good shape for the long term. The workshops are free and open to anyone, not just orchard volunteers. We hope they will bring in some new faces.

Finally, we have been thinking about the longer term. The orchard is still very young, and most of our trees will not produce a real crop for another two or three years. When they do, we will need a plan for the harvest. Who picks the fruit? Who gets to take it home? What happens to the fruit nobody picks? Some groups we have talked to hold a few organized picking days and share the fruit among volunteers and the local food bank. Others let anyone pick at any time. We have not decided yet, and there is no rush, but it is worth starting the conversation now, so that we are ready when the time comes.

There are also some smaller items on our list. We want to replace the logbook box at the gate, which leaked during the last storm. We want to put up a simple sign explaining what the orchard is and how to get involved. We would like to add a bench or two, so that people can sit and enjoy the space. And we want to keep up the flower border along the edge of the lot, which did such a good job of attracting helpful insects last summer.

All of this adds up to a busy year, and we will need help. If you have a skill that might be useful, whether it is carpentry, fundraising, graphic design, or just a strong back, please let us know. If you can only give a few hours over the whole season, that is still welcome. The orchard has always depended on many people each giving a little, and that will not change.

I will post a draft budget and a calendar of work days after our next meeting. In the meantime, if you have any thoughts on the fence, the wet corner, the shed, or anything else in this post, please share them. We are working toward a plan that the whole group can feel good about, and the more voices we hear, the better that plan will be.

Thank you, as always, for being part of this. It is a small project in the scheme of things, a patch of trees behind a library, but it has brought a lot of people together who might never have met otherwise. That, as much as the fruit we hope to pick someday, is the reason we keep doing it. See you at the next work day, and dress warmly, because the mornings out there have been colder than anyone expected this year.
